note: Opens act 2 (Midterm). Table 5.1's semiconductor memory types and the ECC inequality 2^K - 1 >= M + K are used as the book states them; the hamming-check-bits solver implements that same inequality in its equivalent form 2^K >= M + K + 1.

items.stem: A semiconductor memory cell must have three properties. Which of the following is one of them?
items.correct: It can be in one of two stable states, used to represent binary 1 and 0
distractors: It must retain its value after power is removed
It must be readable and writable at the same instant
It must store its value as a voltage rather than a charge
items.rationale: A cell exhibits two stable states, can be written to set its state, and can be read to sense its state. Non-volatility is a property of SOME memory types, not of cells in general — DRAM and SRAM are both volatile and both are built from cells.
items.source: ch-05.md §5.1 — the properties of a memory cell

items.stem: What is the purpose of a memory cell's SELECT terminal?
items.correct: It chooses whether this particular cell participates in the current read or write
distractors: It determines whether the operation is a read or a write
It carries the data value into or out of the cell
It supplies the refresh charge for a dynamic cell
items.rationale: Three terminals: select picks the cell, control indicates read or write, and a third carries data. Confusing select with control is the natural error, and it matters because the select line is what an address decoder drives.

items.stem: How does a DRAM cell store a bit?
items.correct: As charge on a capacitor, whose presence or absence is read as 1 or 0
distractors: In a flip-flop built from cross-connected transistors
As the magnetic polarity of a small ferrite core
As the threshold voltage of a floating-gate transistor
items.rationale: Charge on a capacitor is the defining DRAM mechanism, and the reason DRAM needs refreshing — capacitors discharge naturally. The first distractor is the SRAM cell and the third is flash.

items.stem: Which statement about SRAM is correct?
items.correct: It holds its data as long as power is supplied, with no refreshing required
distractors: It holds its data indefinitely, even without power
It requires refreshing, but less often than DRAM
It stores data as charge, like DRAM, but with a larger capacitor
items.rationale: SRAM is a digital device using the same flip-flop logic as the processor, so it needs no refresh — but it is still VOLATILE. Confusing 'no refresh needed' with 'non-volatile' is the commonest error on this pair.

items.stem: Stallings calls the DRAM cell 'essentially an analog device' even though it stores one bit. Why?
items.correct: The capacitor can hold any charge in a range, and a threshold decides whether it reads as 1 or 0
distractors: It can store fractional values that software interprets as probabilities
Its output voltage varies continuously with the address applied
It uses analog amplifiers rather than logic gates to drive the data line
items.rationale: The stored quantity is continuous; only the INTERPRETATION is binary. That is precisely why charge leaking away eventually crosses the threshold and corrupts the bit, and therefore why refresh exists.
items.source: ch-05.md §5.1 — 'a threshold value determines whether the charge is interpreted as 1 or 0'

items.stem: Why is SRAM less dense and more expensive per bit than DRAM?
items.correct: An SRAM cell needs several transistors in a flip-flop arrangement, where a DRAM cell needs roughly one transistor and a capacitor
distractors: SRAM cells must be physically larger to hold more charge
SRAM requires an extra layer of metallisation for its refresh circuitry
SRAM cells must be spaced further apart to avoid interference
items.rationale: Cell complexity drives density, which drives cost. The second distractor is doubly wrong: SRAM needs no refresh circuitry at all — that is DRAM's burden, and it is one of the few places DRAM pays and SRAM does not.
items.source: ch-05.md §5.1 — SRAM structure, four cross-connected transistors

items.stem: Given their characteristics, why is SRAM used for cache and DRAM for main memory?
items.correct: SRAM is faster but dearer and less dense, so it suits the small fast level; DRAM is cheaper and denser, so it suits the large slow one
distractors: SRAM is non-volatile, so the cache survives a power interruption
DRAM cannot be manufactured in the small capacities a cache needs
SRAM's refresh cycles would be too slow for main memory
items.rationale: This is the memory hierarchy argument applied to two real technologies. The last distractor inverts the refresh property — SRAM has none — and that inversion is worth catching because it appears whenever the two are first compared.

items.stem: In Table 5.1, how is data written into a plain ROM, and can it be erased?
items.correct: Written by masks during fabrication, and erasure is not possible
distractors: Written electrically by the customer, and erased with ultraviolet light
Written electrically at any time, and erased electrically byte by byte
Written by masks, and erased electrically at block level
items.rationale: ROM contents are fixed at manufacture, which is why it is only attractive for high-volume runs. The distractors describe EPROM, EEPROM and flash respectively — the read-mostly family that exists precisely because ROM cannot be changed.

items.correct: By exposing the whole chip to intense ultraviolet light through a window in the package
distractors: Electrically, one byte at a time
Electrically, one block at a time
It cannot be erased once programmed
items.rationale: EPROM erasure is optical and CHIP-LEVEL — all cells return to the same initial state, and each erasure can take up to 20 minutes. EEPROM is electrical and byte-level; flash is electrical and block-level. The granularity is what separates the three.

items.stem: Put these read-only memory types in order of increasing write flexibility, from the one that can never be changed to the one that can be updated in place a byte at a time.
items.rationale: ROM is written by masks at fabrication and cannot be erased. PROM is written electrically, once. EPROM can be erased repeatedly, but only whole-chip and only by ultraviolet light, taking up to 20 minutes. EEPROM is erased electrically at byte level with no removal from the circuit. Each step buys flexibility and pays in cost and density.

items.source: ch-05.md §5.2 — Error Correction, the check-bit inequality

items.stem: In the error-correcting scheme, what does a syndrome word of all zeros indicate?
distractors: An error occurred in one of the check bits and needs no correction
An uncorrectable double-bit error occurred
The data bit at position zero is in error
items.rationale: The syndrome is the bit-by-bit exclusive-OR of the stored and recomputed check bits. All zeros means every position matched. A single 1 bit means a check bit itself was corrupted, and more than one 1 gives the numerical position of the failed DATA bit.
items.source: ch-05.md §5.2 — 'If the syndrome contains all 0s, no error has been detected'

items.stem: The check-bit inequality is 2^K - 1 >= M + K, not 2^K - 1 >= M. Why does K appear on both sides?
items.correct: The check bits are stored alongside the data and can themselves be corrupted, so the syndrome must be able to identify them too
distractors: It reserves extra codes for detecting double-bit errors
It accounts for the syndrome word needing its own parity bit
It compensates for the exclusive-OR losing one bit of information
items.rationale: An error could occur on any of the M data bits OR the K check bits, so the syndrome must distinguish M + K positions plus the no-error case. Dropping the K is the mistake that yields a code one bit too short, and it is silent — the code still works until a check bit fails.
items.source: ch-05.md §5.2 — 'because an error could occur on any of the M data bits or K check bits'
ch-05.md §5.1 — chip organization and module construction

items.stem: What distinguishes SDRAM from traditional DRAM?
items.correct: It exchanges data synchronised to an external clock, so the processor can do other work while the request is serviced
distractors: It transfers data on both the rising and falling clock edges
It stores two bits per cell instead of one
It requires no refresh, unlike traditional DRAM
items.rationale: SDRAM latches the address and responds after a known number of clock cycles, so the master need not wait. The first distractor is DDR, which builds ON SDRAM — the two are often conflated, and the distinction is the point of this item.

items.stem: Put these DRAM interfaces in the order they were developed, from earliest to most recent.
items.rationale: Traditional DRAM is asynchronous: the master must wait an unpredictable time for a response. SDRAM latches the request and responds after a known number of clock cycles, so no wait states are imposed and the master can do other work meanwhile. DDR then transfers on both clock edges. Each step improves the PROTOCOL rather than the array's access time.

items.stem: A memory array is described as needing periodic charge restoration to retain its contents, and as achieving very high density per chip. Which technology is it, and why?
items.correct: DRAM — one transistor and a capacitor per cell gives high density, and the capacitor's leakage forces refresh
distractors: SRAM — its flip-flop cells must be periodically rewritten to stay stable
EEPROM — it is electrically refreshed a byte at a time
Flash — block erasure is a form of refresh
items.rationale: Two clues point the same way: refresh implies charge storage, and high density implies a small cell. Only DRAM has both. An SRAM flip-flop holds its state indefinitely while powered, so the first distractor invents a requirement SRAM does not have.
items.source: ch-05.md §5.1 — dynamic RAM and static RAM
